segments.text: Good morning. Yes, now we can feel the vibe, thank you. So my name is Didier Acouetey

I founded the first executive research firm dedicated to Africa, and we've been recruiting over the last 30 years, African in various sectors, all around the continent from the diaspora, top-level positions, and with branches around the continent. I haven't done this, of course, alone, but with partners. But why did we do this? Because we really were convinced when we were students back in the days in Paris that the most valuable assets, its human resources, its talents.

It's not only having a soul, not mineral resources, but human capacity. So I've been dealing with this talent business for the last 30 years, and again, thanks to Dr. Lassina Zerbo, President Kagame, and the government of Rwanda to host this second edition of the NEISA, and to talk about this important topic about human capital and talent development. This is critical because, you know, today we stand at the threshold of the nuclear era, and the founding question is now whether we can build reactors.

The question is, do we have and can we build the human infrastructure to operate them safely, sustainably on African terms? You know the figures, you know, over 600 million Africans still have no access to electricity, and we need to industrialize the continent. And I've been serving as well over the last eight months as senior advisor to the African Development Bank President to tackle what we call the new African financial architecture, but especially industrialize the continent. And to industrialize this continent, we need energy.

And some of the development banks have decided that energy is not anymore a sector, because it's cross-cutting, it needs to be a pillar of everything we're doing in the continent. So we need energy, basically. And this comes right on time, the SMR challenge, which to be honest can be addressed in Africa, but we need the workforce to design, commission, operate, regulate, and maintain these reactors that don't yet exist at scale in the continent.

So what brings us in this room is really to address this talent challenge and make sure while we industrialize the continent, while we build these SMRs, we have the required skills and talents. And over the last years, we've been seeing some countries, especially China, paving the way with massive investment in this sector, with strong capacity building, where basically when China trains 1.3 million engineers every year, we hardly train 30 to 50,000. So the gap is huge if you want to address the energy demand and industrialization.

I won't be too long, but I will put it in six concrete ways. Number one, or six imperative, the first one is to build knowledge infrastructure. Before building reactors, we need that knowledge, and this is critical.

So we must equip our universities with the right environment, the right professors, the right teachers, and of course set the safety science curricula and regulated training pathways. The second is imperative to make skills transfer mandatory. Every reactor project built on African soil must carry contractual requirements to train local engineers, operators, and regulators as a licensing condition, not a corporate responsibility of the third.
The third one is to triple STEM enrollment within a decade. I gave you some figures. We will need to embark more of our youth in this team.

Going from 10% to 30% of STEM enrollment requires targeted scholarship, a teacher's pipeline, and a serious recovery program for secondary school mathematics. The numbers have been, you know, falling over the years, so we need a really engaging strategy to have more students into STEM. The fourth imperative is to finance the educational ecosystem, not just the power plants.

Nuclear universities, research reactors, safety authorities, and regulatory bodies are not expensive , so we need the same blended public-private finance structure, so otherwise you cannot build this SMR industry. The fifth one is to mobilize every source of talent available, women, youth, and diaspora. In the diaspora, we have thousands of nuclear-qualified engineers and scientists working today in France, United States, Canada, United Kingdom, you name it.
They are a resource. We need to incentivize them to return to build programs remotely. And the sixth one is to leapfrog with digital tools.

You know, AI simulation, digital transactors, remote learning platform means Africa doesn't need to replicate a 15-year Western training pipeline. We can move faster. We can leapfrog what we did in the telecom industry.

Lastly, we need to engage more of the private sector. We need to co-construct with them because they'll be the one co-financing the SMR industry. And the closing, to close my remarks, I would just say that this is a story of structural deficits, less than 3% of global clean energy employment, 1.3 million engineers in China.
You can look at the numbers. We need to do much more. The second is a story of extraordinary and repeatable opportunity.

14 million energy transition jobs possible by 2030, 100 million renewable energy jobs in 2050, and the largest working-age population in the history of humanity arriving on this continent within the next two decades. So the talent is here. The demographic dividend is on its way.

SMR technology is finally within reach. What we owe this generation is the educational infrastructure, the public-private architecture, and the regional coordination to turn that potential into a workforce that is ready when the first African-built SMR comes online. This is not a distant ambition.
It's an urgent operational imperative. Let's build it together. Thank you.

I'd now like to introduce the panel and ask them to join me on the stage. We have Mr. Gashaw Gebeyehu Wolde acting director for the Technical Corporation in Africa at the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Professor Samuel Dampare, Director General at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission. Dr. Sola Talabi, President at Pittsburgh Technical. Professor Lisa Marshall, Director of Outreach, Retention and Engagement in the Department of Nuclear Engineering at NC State University.

And Mr. Alexander Kormishin, Director of the Center for International Partnerships at the Rosatom Corporate Academy. From the IAEA's perspective, what are the most urgent technical assistance priorities for African countries in building the necessary regulatory and operational workforce capacity? Thank you very much,Dr.Tracey. Good morning, everyone.

From the IAEA perspective, there are urgent priorities that need to be addressed. In order to support development of the workforce for the nuclear industry. The first area is strengthening institutional competence alongside technology development and acquisition.

This includes the regulatory infrastructure, legal frameworks, strengthening the safety culture, radiation protection, and a number of other training and capacity building supports that need to be expanded in order to respond to the growing and emerging needs of member states. The second area is there is a priority to continue supporting capacity building in other support areas like cyber security, like also workforce planning and structuring and other training and capacity building in the nuclear value chain. From extraction to fabrication, nuclear island, waste management, grid integration, and also project management.

This has been all highlighted in the IAEA milestones approach and the technical cooperation program also takes it as a key priority supporting member states. While doing that, there is an increased emphasis on long term human resource planning. And there is also emphasis on strengthening regional cooperation through centers of excellences, regional designated centers, harmonization of training standards, and also supporting peer to peer learning.

This takes place in various platforms including the triangular cooperation approach. Areas like enhancing communication and stakeholder engagement are also key and important for strengthening public acceptance, trust and transparency. From the IAEA technical cooperation perspective, it is highly advocated now there should be an increased trust and focus on development of a sustainable and institutional capacity in member states.

Of course, harnessing and focusing on a continental approach and bolstering with strategic cooperation, strategic partnership. In this regard, we are working with renowned universities and also universities within the region as well as outside the region where we can develop collaborative training and capacity building programs. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much. And thank you for exercising that need for a sustainable human capacity development program, something that can see through the nuclear energy development in our country. We talk a lot about recruitment, outreach, finding the new workforce, but there is another part of the discussion in terms of retention.

So I'd like to pass this question on to Professor Dampare. How is Ghana addressing the retention challenge, keeping your skilled workforce available and ready for use? And if possible, can you share some of the lessons learned as you navigated this challenge? Thank you very much, Tracy. And there's a little on your table that I want to resign or something.

I say, oh, so that is a real challenge, a real problem, but we are doing something about it. I will start by saying that I've been involved in capacity building or training for students for some time now. I was once the Vice Dean of our Graduate School of Nuclear and Allied Sciences, going around the country and telling people that, oh, come and do this nuclear stuff.

And then sometimes what they ask you is, so after this education, you can teach them what's next, employment, so to be able to tell them where they can fit. But the bigger picture is that when you have already attracted them and they are with you, they want to leave because of sometimes competitive compensation, salary issues. I think that's one of the major challenges we are facing.

Maybe if you compare those within our country, no, we don't have commercial projects where you think you are going to pay them so well. And if they compare themselves to the oil and gas industry and so on and so forth, they say that, but if something is pulling me elsewhere and I can't get good money, I stay here. So what we are trying to do, even recently I started engaging the authorities, telling them about these compensation issues, that really we need to do something about our salaries.

Otherwise we get up one day and I'll be the only person left. So that is one of the things that we are doing. But apart from remuneration issues and other things, we are also trying to build strong institutions.

You know, when it comes to nuclear stuff, we have the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission, we have the Nuclear Regulatory Authority and the Nuclear Power Ghana. So these institutions that I've mentioned provide career pathways so that if these people graduate, they'll be absorbed by these institutions. So we are building these strong institutions and we don't want institutions to be just there for employment sake, but we are also looking at research and innovation aspect of this.
So people will be encouraged to work in the institutions. So they are there, not at all. We are also doing research, innovation and other things, so they are happy to stay.

And we also try to integrate them, especially the young ones and the highly skilled ones, with the projects that we are doing. For instance, now, if you go to Nuclear Power Ghana, they are in phase two anyway, so that is what they are doing. And we get these young, highly skilled people involved so that the sense of people's ownership is there.

So that is one of the things that we are doing. Another thing is that we are trying to make sure that we provide them with continuous professional training and all that. So working with Ghana, we think that we can achieve this, go to send some of them out there for maybe a scientific visit.

We have expectations, issues and then professional shifts so at least they know that we are there and we can get these opportunities to go to other places, especially advanced countries, to know about what is going on. We are also encouraging the youth, the young ones to be part of their youth network, like Physitech, African generation in nuclear. They see that they are doing a great job.

So we are encouraging young ones to be part of this. Are there women in nuclear power? Yeah, what I did about two years ago is that I appointed one, a woman, for a seminary at Pedu, to see to it that the young, not the young, the women in atomic energy, is trying to bring them together and organize programs. I realized that when it comes to top management, we don't have women there.

So I said, try to mobilize women, I said, what are the challenges there? How can we navigate these things? So that is what I did. The other one, we are designing a one day scholarship, sort of, we allow people to go there, but we bond them. Maybe you have, after your program, you have like five years to work with us.
Maybe by that time we would have also been able to train more people. So that is what we are doing. So I say thank you.

I know it's not an easy question to answer, but it's clear that Ghana has been thinking through this situation. I wanted to talk to Congress a bit. Dr. Talabi, so all countries are thinking about different types of nuclear technologies.

And I would like to know, do the training requirements for SMRs, MMRs differ from those of large reactors? And if yes, can you elaborate how and how countries need to have human capacity development based on what they're looking at? Thank you, Tracey-Ann. And thank you, Naysa, for this tremendous opportunity. And to my co-panelists, it's truly a pleasure to be on this panel.
I'm born and raised in Nigeria. And so for me, this is, it's a homecoming and my first time in Rwanda. And it's just been an absolute blast.

I think everything's been so well-organized and I'm just going to go back and tell people about Rwanda at some point. So to answer your question, great question. I think it addresses one of what I call the five P's.

So the question is on the P for product. But we also have other P's that there's the, on the people, the processes, the physical infrastructure and policies that are different between the large existing reactors and the modular reactors or advanced reactors, micro-reactors that are actually more likely to be deployed in emerging nations. So the product piece is, you know, for SMRs, advanced reactors, how large light water reactors, the existing technologies.

But I want to emphasize that we, to really understand and be able to explore that question, we need to understand the difference in how the existing reactors were developed and how nations like Rwanda would approach the new technology. So the existing reactors built in the West, in Asia, were developed on very robust existing supply chains that were built in some cases, they evolved from military programs like naval nuclear programs that had years and years of history. They also were built on a very robust national research lab complex.

Like in the case of the US, there are six national labs that are focused on nuclear research, Idaho National Labs, India National Labs, the national labs, et cetera. And then they were also built on very robust academic programs, nuclear academic programs. So all of these, that framework, and supply chains also, I think I mentioned that.

So that framework together over the years developed a set of research reactors. And in developing those research reactors, they ran into a lot of problems. Every time they run into some problems, they learn from those issues.

And eventually they mature to a point that they're able to build the first commercial reactor, which actually is in Shippingport, just outside of Pittsburgh, where I live. So when you talk about the first commercial reactor in the US, it actually has decades of military programs, research lab experiments, and at least, I believe, before the Shippingport plant was built, there were at least 60 research reactors that were built. So fast forward to today, an emerging nuclear nation like Rwanda is looking at developing the first, or deploying the first SMR.

They don't have that history, right? And so it's truly first of a kind in many respects. And so it's first of a kind for those five P's in terms of the people, not having had the, perhaps, like a naval nuclear background. It's first of a kind for the supply chain.
It's first of a kind for some of the regulatory processes. It's first of a kind for policy. And certainly based on that, we're then looking at this first of a kind product deployment.

So I think it's really important to understand that even if it's a first of a kind, we are proceeding at significantly more risk, perhaps, than those initial Western deployments because we don't have that framework. However, like the keynote speaker said, it is, we do also have 60 years of advancement, right? And so we don't have to necessarily do things the way that we had done 60 years ago. We can leverage technology.

We can leverage AI significantly. For instance, with regulatory processes, there are a lot of efforts now that are being put into how do we use AI to rapidly develop regulatory artifacts? So there are processes that used to take years that can now potentially be done in days, right? Because it's just, you don't have to dig through thousands of documents to put together a safety case. It can be rapidly developed.

So I think the use and leverage of technology is really gonna be critical. And so for the academic and training programs that we need, I can tell you that I think there's tremendous opportunity there. When I go to the IAEA sometimes, I see my colleagues from Africa come in and get training on reactors that are 60 years old.

And it really frustrates me because I'm thinking, okay, yes, we do have to have a solid understanding of the basics, but these SMRs, microreactors, there are differences in terms of how they're designed, developed, deployed, operated, maintained, and how they'll be decommissioned that are gonna be significantly different from the existing reactors. So yes, we have to use it, we have to leverage technology. We have to appreciate that, an example would be with digitization.

The SMRs and light water reactors are quite different in that the existing reactors are band lag, large analog systems. The new reactors will be digital. And with that, you now have cybersecurity vulnerabilities that are created.

Hence, we need cybersecurity training and cybersecurity risk training, which is something that's not yet emphasized in the curriculum. You can also think about the deployment scenarios in that these SMRs, microreactors are planned to be co-located with other industrial facilities, perhaps data centers co-located with SMRs and microreactors. You now have a new set of safety issues, which is an initiating event from a data center that could affect an SMR and vice versa.

And that's not an existing issue that we have. Existing reactors are typically intentionally set in the middle of nowhere so that if an issue occurs, you don't have those interdependent complexities that cause risk. However, it should also be appreciated that these SMRs and microreactors do have technological advancements that have retired some of the existing concerns like some of the accidents that have occurred in the past, the Fukushima, Chernobyl, Three Mile Island accidents.

Some of those are no longer credible with these new reactors. But again, there are new risks that we have to make sure that we're addressing. And for that reason, in the US, my company established a program called SMART.

It's the Small Modular Advanced Reactor Training, SMART, that is focused on what those gaps are, what the differences are, how we close those gaps. So again, to summarize, there are five Ps that are critical. It's the people, the processes, the physical infrastructure, the policy, and all that then informs the product selection.

Thank you so much. It's clear that in the same way that it's not one size fits all with the nuclear technology that countries are picking, it's also not the same for the training programs. So depending on which direction a country is going, they might need to adapt their training programs to meet the needs of that technology.

So I'll move on to Professor Marshall. So Africa's nuclear future will require not only engineers and scientists, but also professionals in policy, finance, supply chain, project management, entrepreneurship. How can young people from multidisciplinary backgrounds contribute meaningfully to the sector? Thank you, Tracey-Anne.
It's my pleasure to be at NEISA. This is my first and hopefully not my last. I am a child of the African diaspora, born and raised in Trinidad, through Canada, and now in the US.
I think I'm making that loop back. This is my second time to Rwanda. It is, I feel like it's a second home.

I think I said the same thing about Ghana, and I said the same thing about Cape Town…., but I do feel at home here. And it is a community, a nuclear community that goes across the established borders that we have. And earlier in some of the sessions, we talked about regional communities, right? I want to say that we need to flip the question a little bit, right, or that it has two parts.

There's a responsibility by our various organizations, and then there are responsibilities by our next gen and individuals that are looking to make that vertical move into the nuclear space. And also, we tend to talk about the non-STEM individuals, and I'd like to change the language a bit. These individuals are STEM adjacent.

And when we think about our educational system, we tend to, you know, in the early years, I'm thinking back to primary school and to secondary school, everything is together, right? There is not that distinction between the math, the science, the physical sciences, and your history, your English, et cetera. You're getting the parts thereof, and they are still collectively together. And then when we step into community college and or to universities, you've got to pick a particular route, right? You've got to pick a particular major.

And I think that has done us some disservice in some ways, not to have it connected in some way, shape or form. But let me go back to this two-part question in particular, that that multidisciplinary narrative needs to be articulated by various organizations. The companies that are looking to attract individuals, the professional organizations that are also looking to act as a professional development, career development community, and then also the population in general, right? As we're talking about what we need to move to the next step, to expand our industries, expand our social network, that they're all connected, right? And then we need to continually articulate that.

And then to more clearly speak about the career pathways. It's less about the pipeline in my estimation, and then also the experiences that I've had in the industry. And it's more about those pathways because individuals come in and you have something in mind and with the experiences, with the education, with the on-the-job training, you're then figuring out, well, I had in mind this particular path set out for me, but it's more of a journey.

And that realization, you're maneuvering through the industry, through the landscape, through the community itself. And then to do this through professional organizations, through training, as well as educational spaces. And then for us to have more intentional mentions and activities and programming that is scaffolding, right? So you start as an entry point into the industry, but what are we doing within the industry to show and prepare individuals for new experiences, right? And something that we haven't really talked about is kind of that realistic forecasting and articulation thereof.

So there's a responsibility by our organizations to have a timeline and it can be dynamic. It must be dynamic. But for us to be realistically chatting with our STEM adjacent, our young individuals that are in training and educational programs, and then those that want to make the transition from another sector.

It really is about relationship building. This is long-term, right? And to start early and to be very intentional often as we move forward. Now, the other part of it, which is really your question, right? Is looking at the students themselves and from working with students from, gosh, primary, secondary, community college, and then undergraduate programs and graduate programs.

It's to say to students that this is a sector that you want to enter in and therefore our active participation thereof, right? So understanding the landscape and then keeping up to date. And organizations have gotten better and we're doing better and getting better at doing that in a way of having these online platforms that are up to date and share what that landscape looks like. So for someone who is now coming in, in addition to having organizations speak to specifically individuals, there is also the onus to then for us to take a look at what does the landscape look like? Are there some companies and company alerts that I should be signing up for? Are there news wires that are out there that are pushing information out and have I signed up for it? So every morning there is additional information that is coming to me to make some informed decisions as to what I want to do.

And I say all of this because there is access, but there's also agency for one to have success and to wait for organizations, not necessarily to push them. Yeah, push them, right? A number of the professional organizations have been doing that and we've gotten better. It's a work in progress on the journey that we're currently on together.

I think I'm gonna stop there just to say that this is a partnership and it's multidimensional directional and it's multidimensional. And there is a need for STEM and STEM adjacent individuals in this field. Organizations have to do a whole lot better in their forecasting and their articulation of the narrative about where exactly this journey is heading and then students, and I say students in the broadest sense of the word also have to take that onus as well.

I guess I just wanted to add one other little part, right? I'm not a nuclear engineer, right? I'm a geographer by training, energy geography as well. And I had come into the industry coming from the point of view of outreach retention and engagement and there was a learning curve and it was a huge learning curve. But the individuals at the organizations that I joined took the time, right, to assist me.

And I also asked the necessary questions accordingly and joined organizations such as the American Nuclear Society and the Women in Nuclear and used those platforms, NEISA, IEA, WNA, the World Nuclear Association, et cetera, just to get an understanding of exactly what that landscape looks like. And then the short courses, right? And the longer courses and education, for me, it was at the graduate level because I wanted to fit into this sector. I saw the benefits there and that my skill sets could fit.

Now, if I waited until they came knocking at the door, I think I'd still be there waiting for them to come knocking at the door, so to speak. And you have an opportunity as well through the professional organizations to then chart the direction of those organizations as well. So I started rolling up my sleeves and doing outreach work in the American Nuclear Society, joining the various divisions that were specific to me on the environmental sciences side, in addition to the education training and workforce development division and some of the other committees that existed.

And to see that you are part and parcel, giving you more and more responsibilities. And many of you all out there know that I am the immediate past president of the American Nuclear Society. So there's a place for each one of us and that agency as we move forward to push the organizations and then roll up our sleeves and be that force that is very important.

Thank you. I like the term STEM adjacent because the reality of the field is that you might come in as a STEM professional, but that's not what your career evolves into. I came in as a STEM professional and I'm definitely STEM adjacent at this point in time.

So we'd like to move on to Mr. Kormichin. So as you think about the training programs and developing the youth, how does your organization work with the youth to develop the workforce? Thank you very much, Dr.Tracey. And thank you for moderating this amazing panel.
My name is Alexander. This is also my second time here in Rwanda. So I compliment the speaker in your country.

Thank you very much for welcoming me here. I actually had a plan for my speech, but then listening to each of you, I thought that maybe I should come from a little bit other point where we are addressing training. So basically before building a project, maybe there is a need to build a dream.

And whenever we are talking about a dream, of course it has to do with the nation, the country, because nuclear infrastructure projects are large, long term. But in order to build capacity, you have to build a dream for everyone, especially young people in the country. And I believe this is where we are focusing our workforce development programs at Rosatom and the division where I come from, Rosatom Corporate Academy, where we are addressing leadership and management.

I guess many of you are aware that Rosatom is a large logical leader and we are covering the full cycle of local projects. And whenever we are addressing capacity building, it is, it takes creativity. It takes a lot of work to address the younger generation.

So you see that young people are changing and not only young people, those who are in this industry. So it is worth a lot of effort to retain them because a lot of things are happening on the labor market, new things like AI showing up and of course it leads a lot to a safe interest. We are doing a lot in terms of building capacity through universities, partner universities.

We're very proud to work with the University of Rwanda where we have a joint program with our Russian university, MEPI. And I understand that over a hundred young people from Rwanda are currently getting education there in Russia to come back here and the homeland to work to build an industry. And with all of that, whenever we are talking about the younger generation, we understand that so-called universities education and also in-house education training programs that were built at Rosatom through our technical academy and corporate academy are really not enough.

So, in order to save that interest, in order to instill a dream, we managed to build a number of other programs for sure. And we're currently working through different initiatives like I'd say a direct dialogue between the corporation, Rosatom and the younger generation. We have even created a certain youth advisory board for our DG who is in constant dialogue with the young leaders from all over the world.

And he practically discusses with these young people how Rosatom is a global corporation for the work together with the younger generation, with the young people. And these young people are, wouldn't say just only students. So we'll listen to the younger generation, the ones who already succeeded a lot in the age where they are.

They are advisors, they are building projects on their own also as part of different initiatives. So we are in Africa, I'm talking about African YGN in this case. So young people have a lot of opportunities beyond their direct dialogue with corporations, universities so they can build a career on their own.

And we have a lot to do about saving their interest. We have to do a lot about making sure that they are with us and the message that I wanted to leave and also a question often for young people here at the audience, what's your dream about building a nuclear power plant in your sector here in your homeland? I will give you just a couple of ideas. So maybe it's about national welfare of your country, welfare of your families, or maybe make your country stand out in terms of industries like AI, quantum technologies or medicine, because it has all to do with nuclear energy and nuclear science.
So with this, I'd like to pass the floor to Dr.Tracey. Thank you very much for the opportunity. Thank you.

And thank you for talking about the creativity that cannot be ignored, that is needed as we think about this development directly engaging the youth and seeing what is their vision too. And so I'd like to ask my panelists to just give some closing remarks, what they would like to leave you with as we end this session. So we start with Mr. Wolde.

Thank you very much, Tracey. Regarding human resource development, a coordinating infrastructure in pipelines, training standards, as well as specialized center of excellences would bolster the expansion and possibilities for building human resources for the nuclear future in Africa. In this regard, building a shared nuclear talent ecosystem would be an appropriate direction to be pursued.
Thank you. Professor Dampare. Thank you very much, Tracey.

We are all talking about workforce development and we know that a highly skilled workforce is needed for a successful nuclear power program. And if that is the case, I know it cannot be done by one country alone. We need to work together, share resources.

For example, if you come to Ghana, we have Yitu Center, that is New Scale Energy Exploration Center, which we can make available to all Africans who are interested in SMR technology. To come and have a research reactor, go to South Africa, the operating nuclear power plant in Egypt is expanding. Egypt is also constructing a Moroccan.

So what I want to say is that let's work together within the African side. We can still collaborate with our colleagues in advanced countries, but as Africans, we can also work together within these limited resources that we have. We can share the infrastructure that we have, then we avoid duplication.

And then the young ones, I will say they are our future, they are present. And we want to embrace, let's work together and make Africa proud and let our nuclear power program proceed. Let me take this opportunity to thank the organizers for inviting me.

I'm very grateful to Dr Fidel, now the CEO of RAEB, and Dr. Lassina Zerbo for their hospitality. Thank you. So reactor deployment in the Western Asia will be different from reactor deployment in Africa and in emerging nations.

So we need to place an African lens or a nation specific lens on deployment. And it's different because the Western programs were developed on a very robust military program, very robust national university, nuclear programs, national research labs, and very robust and well-established supply chains. Without that benefit, we have to ensure that when we look at those five key issues that I mentioned in terms of the people, the processes, the physical infrastructure, the products and the policies, that we are truly looking at it with an African lens or a, in this case, Rwanda specific lens.

An example of this would be in technology selection. An additional issue that we have in Africa is job creation, workforce development, supply chain development, and ensuring that these programs are sustainable in the long term. Hence, we would want to select products that ensure that we are able to eventually take on the supply chain and long-term fabrication and production of components that may inform perhaps smaller reactors that are more accessible to the local supply chain than the really large reactors where essentially you only have, you have oligopolies, where it's maybe three or four companies across the world that can provide some of these components.

But as you make the components smaller, there essentially is a guy in your city that can produce some of those components. And so, again, I think the main point I'd like to make is that there really is a need to ensure that we are placing an African specific lens on those five Ps. Again, thank you for this tremendous opportunity and I hope to be back in Rwanda.

I have to agree with all of my colleagues and their comments made thus far. It's, to me, especially since I work with individuals in the educational system pre-college and then also college, it's about intentional communities within nuclear and that those communities are looking at the STEM disciplines as well as the STEM adjacent. And there's not that separation in what we do to advance the journey so that there's always also a need for us to be very intentional in our various organizations to be inclusive, to be seeing the connections and the multidisciplinarity of what we do with regards to nuclear nations.
